DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11737.setting: Three inpatient mental health wards across two hospitals
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11737.standard: NICE guidance and local trust policies on cardiovascular assessment, ECG, metabolic monitoring and risk–benefit documentation when prescribing antipsychotics

cycle1.result: BP, heart rate and weight recorded in 19/20; ECG on admission in 8; ECG before or within 72 hours of antipsychotic start in 3; QTc documented in 6; HbA1c checked in 11; ongoing metabolic monitoring in 7; no documented cardiovascular risk–benefit discussion in any case.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11737.other_findings: Medication was reviewed regularly at MDT meetings for all patients. Suggested actions include staff awareness, prescribing checklists and electronic prompts.

DOI:10.1136/emermed-2022-rcem2.49.setting: All Scottish centres with Code Red activations for major trauma (national audit)

cycle1.result: 56 activations; pre-hospital TXA 70%; ED arrival to CRC transfusion 9 mins; ED arrival to FFP 50 mins; clotting screen order to result 119 mins; survival to discharge 63%.

cycle2.result: 96 activations; 77 (93%, n=93) received pre-hospital TXA; median ED arrival to CRC transfusion 4 minutes (IQR 0–17) and to FFP 16 minutes (IQR 5–28); median ED arrival to FBC result 70 mins and clotting 74 mins; 65 (68%) survived to discharge.

DOI:10.1136/emermed-2022-rcem2.49.other_findings: A middle audit (1 Nov 2015–31 Dec 2017, 66 activations) was also compared; pre-hospital transfusions rose (16, 48, 73) and CRC and FFP wastage increased. Median 999 call to Code Red activation was 80 minutes.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keaa111.004.topic: Patient involvement in national early inflammatory arthritis audit results
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keaa111.004.setting: Rheumatology department, Lancashire & South Cumbria NHS Foundation Trust, Preston
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keaa111.004.standard: National Early Inflammatory Arthritis Audit (NEIAA) seven quality standards

cycle1.result: Significant room for improvement across all seven quality standards (figures not given).

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keaa111.004.intervention: Results shared with MDT and an NRAS patient support group (45 patients and carers), driver diagrams developed and a patient waiting-area poster produced.
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keaa111.004.other_findings: Patients suggested community awareness posters, an awareness day, more lunchtime meetings and an Expert Patient role; they advised removing alarming statistics from the poster.

DOI:10.1093/bjd/ljaf085.270.topic: Contact allergy to alkyl glucosides on patch testing
DOI:10.1093/bjd/ljaf085.270.setting: Eleven patch testing centres in the UK and Ireland

cycle1.result: 57 patients (2.1%) had a positive reaction to at least one alkyl glucoside; DG 5% pet. positive in 36 (1.3%), LG 3% aq. in 24 (0.9%).

DOI:10.1093/bjd/ljaf085.270.other_findings: Six centres testing 1099 patients in a cosmetic series found a further 14 (1.3%) positives. Concomitant positivity between petrolatum and aqueous preparations was variable, and irritant reactions were frequent.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.358.topic: MRI requesting and reporting in axial spondyloarthritis
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.358.setting: Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust, inflammatory back pain MRI protocol
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.358.standard: ASAS guidance on requesting and reporting MRI in suspected axial spondyloarthritis

cycle1.result: Requests: age in 11 (11.4%), sex in 6 (3.8%), HLA-B27 in 35 (22.2%), back pain duration in 30 (18.9%), suspected diagnosis in 149 (94.3%). Reports: bone marrow oedema mentioned in 128 (81.0%), fat metaplasia in 10 (6.3%), statement on whether 'in keeping with axSpA' in 98 (62.0%).

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.358.other_findings: Chronic structural changes were mentioned in only 82 (51.2%) of reports. Joint rheumatology–radiology work is ongoing with a re-audit planned.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keac133.015.topic: Steroid emergency card and adrenal insufficiency advice
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keac133.015.setting: Royal National Hospital for Rheumatic Diseases, Royal United Hospitals, Bath; new giant cell arteritis cases
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keac133.015.standard: National Patient Safety Alert (August 2020) on steroid emergency cards and adrenal insufficiency risk

cycle1.result: No patients given steroid emergency cards at first visit (4 during follow-up); 5/90 given written information on adrenal insufficiency risk at first visit; 1/90 given information on symptoms; none given sick day rules at first visit (9 during follow-up).

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keac133.015.intervention: Dedicated GCA clinics and improved follow-up, standardised written steroid information and personalised reduction plans, education sessions for medical and nursing teams, and electronic prescribing of emergency cards (being incorporated).
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keac133.015.other_findings: Inconsistent follow-up pathways may have compounded the problem. Re-audit planned for January 2022.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keab247.018.topic: Treatment pathway before prostanoid therapy in Raynaud's and digital ulcers
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keab247.018.setting: Rheumatology day unit, Freeman Hospital, Newcastle upon Tyne
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keab247.018.standard: NHS England 2015 commissioning policy pathway for digital ulcers in systemic sclerosis

cycle1.result: Prior trials: CCB 77.4%, ACEi/ARB 41.1%, fluoxetine 9.59%, sildenafil 87.1%, tadalafil 25.8%; 22.6% of SSc patients had tried bosentan; only 2 SSc patients (6.45%) had trialled all pathway drugs before prostanoid.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keab247.018.other_findings: Mean 5.92 epoprostenol infusions per patient per year, estimated £2700 per patient per year versus about £1350 for first-year bosentan with monitoring.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11742.setting: Mulberry Ward, acute adult psychiatric inpatient ward, Scunthorpe
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11742.standard: NICE NG10 (2015); traffic-light compliance green ≥80%, orange 60–79%, red <60%

cycle1.result: 37 RT incidents in 17 patients; seclusion used in 30%; compliance figures not given.

cycle2.result: 79 RT incidents in 10 patients; seclusion fell to 5%; NICE compliance remained excellent for risk assessment, patient rights and documentation, but post-RT monitoring, debriefing, medication review and incident reporting remained below standard.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11742.other_findings: Advance directives were absent in both audits. RT frequency among women rose from 2.2 to 10.5 incidents per patient, and lorazepam became the main agent (43% to 69.6%).

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2017-314585.24.setting: Outpatient and community patients receiving melatonin from hospital pharmacy
DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2017-314585.24.standard: Regular clinic review of melatonin treatment (efficacy, dose, duration)

cycle1.result: 238 (59%) had melatonin reviewed at follow-up; 81 (20%) attended clinic without documented review; 42 (10%) on long-term melatonin not seen for over a year; 39 (10%) newly started not followed up.

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2017-314585.24.other_findings: Of those without review, 52 (64%) had failed to attend clinic. 26 (6.4%) were on other sedatives concurrently; re-audit planned for end of 2016.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10368.topic: Medication safety and errors on psychiatric wards
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10368.setting: West Ward, adult mental health inpatient ward
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10368.standard: Ward medication practice audit domains (including MHRA alerts, controlled drugs, record keeping, prescribing and administration)

cycle1.result: Baseline audit showed significant errors across multiple medication safety domains (figures not given).

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10368.intervention: Three PDSA cycles over six months: targeted training for doctors and nurses, standardised documentation templates, revised induction, controlled drug procedure review and a system for recording MHRA alerts.

cycle2.result: 51% reduction in the total number of medication errors over six months.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10368.other_findings: Largest improvements were in prescribing technicalities, administration errors and controlled drug management; follow-up audits showed the reduction was sustained.

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2016-311535.15.standard: 90% adherence to empirical anti-infective guidelines; 90% indication recorded; 90% duration or review date recorded; 95% initial doses per children's dose table

cycle1.result: Guideline adherence 40/41 (98%); indication recorded 40/42 (95%); duration or review date recorded 26/42 (62%); initial doses per dose table 67/69 (97%).

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2016-311535.15.other_findings: Compared with a 2013 audit, guideline adherence rose from 72% and indication recording from 16%; duration recording remained below target. Proposed actions include electronic prescribing prompts, an updated antibiotic app and compulsory junior doctor teaching.

DOI:10.1192/j.eurpsy.2026.10969.topic: Diabetes care and education in severe mental illness
DOI:10.1192/j.eurpsy.2026.10969.setting: Broadmoor Hospital, secure forensic psychiatric hospital
DOI:10.1192/j.eurpsy.2026.10969.standard: NICE guideline and Public Health guideline PH38 (Type 2 diabetes: prevention in people at high risk)

cycle1.result: 71% of inpatients with type 2 diabetes reported never being offered a structured education course; 54% of nurses had received diabetes training, only 21% within the past year (20.7% staff response rate from 106).

DOI:10.1192/j.eurpsy.2026.10969.other_findings: Nearly half of nurses were unsure of guidelines and 43% cited lack of training as a barrier. Recommendations include mandatory nurse training and a structured patient education programme such as DESMOND.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10660.setting: Multiple mental health hospital sites (acute, PICU, rehabilitation, learning disability, personality disorder units), London and South region
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10660.standard: NHS England Clinical Governance Framework (2022) and local STEELL agenda standards

cycle1.result: Qualitative findings only: progress in safety, patient experience and activities; improvement needed in digital tracking of engagement and MDT participation in governance meetings (no figures given).

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10660.other_findings: Recommendations include standardising incident reporting, better AWOL and contraband security, and sharing best practice; a follow-up audit is planned.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11410.topic: Delirium recognition and screening before psychiatry referral
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11410.setting: Tertiary care teaching hospital; referrals from Medicine, Surgery, Obstetrics and Gynaecology, Orthopaedics and ICU
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11410.standard: CAM-ICU delirium screening before psychiatry referral

cycle1.result: 82/130 (63%) referrals for suspected psychosis were delirium; CAM-ICU use 0%; mean time to delirium management 22 hours.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11410.intervention: Four-week CAM-ICU training: didactic sessions (Medicine, Surgery), bedside demonstrations (ICU, Orthopaedics), and quick-reference materials with brief ward teaching (Obstetrics and Gynaecology).

cycle2.result: Misdiagnosis fell to 39/126 (31%); CAM-ICU uptake 56%; mean time to delirium management 11 hours.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11410.other_findings: Bedside training gave the highest uptake (ICU 72%, Orthopaedics 65%); orthopaedic misdiagnosis fell from 62% to 25%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.234.setting: MHSOP community mental health team, Bassetlaw Hospital
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.234.standard: Royal College of Psychiatrists, GMC and NHS England guidance; Mobile and Remote Access Work and Consent to Examination and Treatment standards

cycle1.result: Remote consultation documented in 81%; consent documented in 57%; addressed concerns documented in 90%; about 40% met standards for management plan documentation.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.234.other_findings: Communication, mental state examination and risk assessment were well documented in about 50–70%. A remote consultation letter template is being developed.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11394.setting: The Harbour, 154-bed mental health hospital (general adult, older adult, dementia and PICU wards)
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11394.standard: Mental Capacity Act (2005), MCA Code of Practice, Trust MCA policy and NICE NG97; target ≥80% of assessments meeting all components

cycle1.result: Decision and time specificity 100%; diagnostic test 77.5%; functional components 70% each; clinical reasoning 60%; correct template use 67.5%; decision-specific framing 60%; outcome stated 92.5%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11394.intervention: 30-minute targeted teaching for resident doctors on MCA principles and the capacity template, reinforced through MDT discussions, handovers and optional quick-reference guidance.

cycle2.result: Diagnostic test 95%; understand 92.5%, retain 90%, use/weigh 90%, communicate 100%; clinical reasoning, template use and decision-specific framing 92.5%; outcome 97.5%.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keaf142.251.setting: Rheumatology unit, Airedale NHS Trust, Keighley
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keaf142.251.standard: GIRFT (Getting It Right First Time) guidance on rheumatology referrals

cycle1.result: 134 of 674 referrals rejected; 101/134 (75.3%) rejected as more appropriate for MSK/pain services or atypical for RMD; 52/134 (37.9%) advised further assessment or investigations in primary care.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keaf142.251.other_findings: 17 (12.6%) were re-referred with more information; 15 were seen and 5 were diagnosed with inflammatory disease. Recommendations include GP training, standardised referral protocols and referral templates or checklists.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.219.setting: Rheumatology, University College London Hospitals, fast-track pathway including PET-CT
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.219.standard: British Society for Rheumatology audit tool standards for suspected GCA

cycle1.result: All reviewed within 3 days (95% by next day); all started on corticosteroids with FBC and ESR; all with visual symptoms given high-dose steroids and ophthalmology review (60% same day); 95% had baseline glucose, 75% vitamin D checked, 70% DEXA; of confirmed GCA, 54% had documented written information and 77% safety-netting advice.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.219.other_findings: 76% had PET-CT (56% positive) and 95% temporal artery ultrasound (11% positive); 7 patients (33%) had negative ultrasound but positive PET-CT. Only 1 patient (4.8%) had temporal artery biopsy.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2024.644.topic: Antipsychotic prescribing and monitoring in young people with eating disorders
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2024.644.setting: Children and Young People (CAMHS) Eating Disorder Service covering York, Scarborough, Harrogate and Northallerton
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2024.644.standard: RCPsych Medical Emergencies in Eating Disorders (May 2022) and local TEWV guidelines

cycle1.result: Physical health monitoring 100%; blood-test monitoring 17%; medication information given 50%; unlicensed indication protocol followed 13%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2024.644.intervention: Spreadsheet to monitor antipsychotic prescriptions and advice on documenting unlicensed indications and providing medication information.

cycle2.result: Physical health monitoring 100%; blood-test monitoring 100%; medication information 67%; unlicensed indication protocol 0%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2024.644.other_findings: All patients were on olanzapine for distress/rumination; psychiatric follow-up and medication review were regular in both audits. Patients from the first audit were excluded from the re-audit.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keaa111.007.topic: Biologic home delivery stock checks and cost saving

cycle1.result: 133/168 patients answered; home stock 0 to 12 weeks; repeat prescriptions delayed in 62 patients by 1 to 8 weeks, a theoretical saving of £13,546.585 (6.5% of the monthly anti-TNF cost of £208,099.94).

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keaa111.007.intervention: Biologic patient education programme launched and patients encouraged to contact the biologic coordinator if non-compliant.
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keaa111.007.other_findings: Reasons for excess stock included infection (20), holiday (6), forgetting (7) and delivery delays or double delivery (3).

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.024.setting: Rheumatology, Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust, London
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.024.standard: BSR guidance (at least 6-monthly review) and a local guideline for annual bDMARD prescribing

cycle1.result: 233/644 (36.2%) eligible patients switched to annual prescribing; 6/233 (2.6%) flared and 1/233 (0.43%) had a significant blood abnormality; 177 (43.1%) met criteria but were not switched.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.024.intervention: Local guideline moving suitable patients from 6-monthly to annual bDMARD prescriptions.
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.024.other_findings: Annual prescribing patients had fewer contacts (>1 appointment 7.7% v 28.7%; >1 blood test 20% v 36.9%). Past audits 2017–2022 showed bDMARD prescriptions rose 76%.

DOI:10.1192/j.eurpsy.2026.10844.topic: Smoking status and cessation support in psychiatric inpatients
DOI:10.1192/j.eurpsy.2026.10844.setting: Mount Carmel Hospital, psychiatric inpatient admissions
DOI:10.1192/j.eurpsy.2026.10844.standard: Documentation of smoking status, cessation advice or referral, and medication adjustment for smoking status change

cycle1.result: Smoking status documented in 87.7%; 113 (51.6%) current smokers; only one discharge letter mentioned cessation advice or referral; no documented medication adjustments for smoking status.

DOI:10.1192/j.eurpsy.2026.10844.other_findings: Smoking was associated with male sex, younger age, secondary education and alcohol use disorders (89% smokers, OR 15).

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11843.topic: Medical referral and follow-up for psychiatric inpatients
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11843.setting: Department of Psychiatry, Gulab Devi Teaching Hospital, Lahore
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11843.standard: Good clinical practice for managing medical comorbidities in psychiatric inpatients

cycle1.result: IM referral made in 65.7%; indication documented 78.3%; investigations attached 60.9%; same-day referral 39.1%; IM review documented 42.9%; recommendations implemented 31.4%; complete loop 28.6%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11843.intervention: Standardised IM referral proforma, reminders to junior doctors, combined verbal and written handover of IM advice, and a ward-round checklist.

cycle2.result: IM referral 88.6%; indication 93.5%; investigations 87.1%; same-day referral 71.0%; IM review documented 80.0%; plans 74.3%; recommendations implemented 71.4%; complete loop 68.6%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11843.other_findings: Audit ran over a 4-month period with interventions over 3–4 months.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keaa111.009.topic: Temporal artery ultrasound for suspected giant cell arteritis
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keaa111.009.setting: Vascular ultrasound unit and rheumatology, Dudley Group NHS Foundation Trust

cycle1.result: 9 (35%) ultrasound diagnostic of GCA; 10 (38%) had biopsy with 100% concordance between ultrasound and biopsy.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keaa111.009.intervention: Training of vascular sonographers in temporal and axillary artery scanning (meeting, co-scanning, visit to Oxford unit, image and report review) before starting service scanning.

cycle2.result: Diagnostic, equivocal and negative findings in 4, 2 and 17; no ultrasound-positive patient had biopsy; 3 ultrasound-negative biopsies were all negative.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keaa111.009.other_findings: Median steroid duration before ultrasound was 1 day versus 6.5 days before biopsy.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11658.setting: Northamptonshire Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust inpatient personality disorder pathway
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11658.standard: NHFT Complex Emotional Needs guideline: pre-admission goals, care plan and engagement contract within 24 hours, consultant review within 72 hours, admission under 14 days

cycle1.result: Admission goals documented within 24 hours in 57%; engagement contracts in 9.5%; discharge dates within 24 hours in 48%; consultant review within 72 hours in 48%; only 21% stayed ≤2 weeks and 26% stayed 5 weeks or longer.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11658.other_findings: About half of referrals lacked clearly documented admission goals. Recommendations include Structured Clinical Management training, group supervision with community PD services and a re-audit.

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2016-311535.39.setting: Paediatric surgical inpatients and discharge prescriptions
DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2016-311535.39.standard: Local 2012 perioperative pain guideline (dosing by ideal body weight) and BNFC; 100% compliance with weight and height documentation, ideal-weight dosing, separate IV prescribing and 48-hour IV-to-oral review

cycle1.result: Weight recorded on 84% of inpatient and 94% of discharge prescriptions; height never documented; IV/PO prescribed together in 32 inpatients; 20 of 52 on IV paracetamol not reviewed at 48 hours (only 3 appropriate).

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2016-311535.39.intervention: Feedback led to amended local guidelines in 2015 (dosing by lean body mass and ideal weight; maximum 75 mg/kg/day).
DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2016-311535.39.other_findings: Sample was 100 inpatient and 35 discharge prescriptions. Overweight or obese children received doses up to 33 mg/kg/dose on discharge.

DOI:10.1093/bjd/ljae090.405.setting: AI-enabled NHS teledermatology skin cancer pathways; 10 NHS consultant teledermatologists
DOI:10.1093/bjd/ljae090.405.standard: NHS England teledermatology audit and quality control standards (no target stated)

cycle1.result: 90% of dermatologists missed two to four high-risk malignancies; management sensitivity 78.3% (95% CI 70.2–84.8) and specificity 47.5% (95% CI 39.3–55.8); Fleiss' kappa 0.43.

DOI:10.1093/bjd/ljae090.405.intervention: Anonymised results discussed in a forum with personalised feedback to each dermatologist.
DOI:10.1093/bjd/ljae090.405.other_findings: Describes the Teledermatology Audit Risk Scoring System (TARSS). Authors are employed by the AI provider.

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2017-314585.26.topic: Enoxaparin prescribing and anti-Xa monitoring in children

cycle1.result: 71% (n=17) of therapeutic prescriptions dosed per BNFc; 35% had anti-Xa within 36 hours; 71% of levels taken 4–6 hours post dose; 82% (n=11) out-of-range levels led to dose change, 56% (n=9) rechecked within 24 hours; 76% (n=25) prophylactic prescriptions per BNFc.

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2017-314585.26.other_findings: 93% (n=42) of prescriptions were whole-number doses. Local guidelines are to be developed with re-audit 12 months after publication; indication was often poorly documented.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.379.setting: Same Day Emergency Care, North Middlesex University Hospital (district general hospital), London
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.379.standard: BSR and GIRFT guidelines for GCA assessment and management

cycle1.result: Steroids 34%; rheumatology referral 55%; temporal artery ultrasound 15%; CRP 92%; median time to eye clinic 2 days.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.379.intervention: Trust SDEC GCA pathway guideline, streamlined temporal artery ultrasound order on IT system, local teaching, pathway poster in clinic rooms and Southend GCA probability score.

cycle2.result: Steroids 54%; rheumatology referral 77%; temporal artery ultrasound 77% (p < 0.001); CRP 100%; median time to eye clinic 1 day.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.379.other_findings: Time to rheumatology assessment did not change significantly (1 to 1.5 days). A GCA probability score >12 had an AUC of 0.978.

DOI:10.1093/bjd/ljae090.069.setting: AI-enabled NHS teledermatology skin cancer pathways; 10 NHS consultant teledermatologists
DOI:10.1093/bjd/ljae090.069.standard: NHS England teledermatology audit and quality control standards (no target stated)

cycle1.result: 90% of dermatologists missed two to four high-risk malignancies; management sensitivity 78.3% (95% CI 70.2–84.8) and specificity 47.5% (95% CI 39.3–55.8); Fleiss' kappa 0.43.

DOI:10.1093/bjd/ljae090.069.intervention: Anonymised results discussed in a forum with personalised feedback to each dermatologist.
DOI:10.1093/bjd/ljae090.069.other_findings: Describes the Teledermatology Audit Risk Scoring System (TARSS); same abstract as BT07. Authors are employed by the AI provider.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/kead104.255.setting: Nurse-led telephone gout clinic, Craigavon Area Hospital (district general hospital)
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/kead104.255.standard: Clinic protocol based on BSR guidance; serum urate <360 µmol/L (<300 µmol/L with erosions or tophi)

cycle1.result: Mean serum urate 509 µmol/L at referral and 322 µmol/L at discharge; all offered and took prophylaxis (85.8% for 3–6 months); 95% had ≤2 flares; no ED attendances for gout.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/kead104.255.other_findings: Mean 3.38 appointments before discharge; lower urate-lowering doses than expected were needed. The telephone model struggled with patients needing an interpreter.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.228.setting: Meridian Ward, older adult functional inpatient ward
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.228.standard: Trust guidance: 3-monthly sodium levels for patients on antidepressants at risk of hyponatraemia

cycle1.result: 11/13 (85%) at-risk patients on antidepressants had 3-monthly sodium levels; only 2 (15%) had a plan for GP sodium monitoring in the discharge summary.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2021.228.other_findings: 3 patients had antidepressant-related hyponatraemia (one with seizure); 1 had no documented plan. Re-audit recommended in 6–12 months.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keaa111.162.topic: Pulmonary hypertension screening in systemic sclerosis
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keaa111.162.standard: Every SSc patient screened annually with echocardiography or NT pro-BNP (European Society of Cardiology)

cycle1.result: 65% screened, all by echocardiography.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keaa111.162.intervention: NT pro-BNP introduced as an adjunct to echocardiography in 2014.

cycle2.result: 88% screened; 25% had echocardiogram and 83% NT pro-BNP; 63% screened by NT pro-BNP only.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keaa111.162.other_findings: Only 6 new PH cases in 1476 patient-years, and all 3 PAH cases came from symptom-driven echocardiograms. Annual screening cost per patient fell from £82 (2014) to £59 (2018).

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11848.topic: Antipsychotic physical health monitoring in children and young people
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11848.standard: NICE-recommended physical health monitoring at baseline, 6 weeks, 12 weeks and 6-monthly for antipsychotics

cycle1.result: Complete baseline monitoring 0% (44.4% had at least one parameter); 6-week weight 22.2%; complete 12-week monitoring 22.2%; across 25 six-monthly windows height 20.0%, weight 20.0%, BP/HR 16.0%, bloods 20.0%, waist circumference 0%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11848.other_findings: No six-monthly window contained all recommended measures, but all patients had some ongoing monitoring and no related adverse outcomes were found.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11157.setting: Five inpatient rehabilitation wards, Royal Edinburgh Hospital
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11157.standard: NICE guidance and local shared-care protocols for lithium monitoring

cycle1.result: Urine ACR absent in all patients; serum calcium and thyroid function missed in about 60%; over 10% of results supratherapeutic; renal function not consistently rechecked after high levels.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11157.other_findings: Several patients had overdue lithium, renal or thyroid tests. Planned next steps are standardised lithium order sets and MDT education.

DOI:10.1192/j.eurpsy.2026.10588.standard: NICE NG222: documented suicidal ideation enquiry (95%) and antidepressants not first-line for less-severe depression without patient preference (90%)

cycle1.result: Suicidal ideation enquiry documented in 17/20 (85%); non-drug first-line treatment for less-severe depression in 9/11 (81.8%).

DOI:10.1192/j.eurpsy.2026.10588.other_findings: Proposed EMIS prompts and templates plus staff training, with re-audit in 12 months.

cycle1.result: Mean Y-BOCS improved from 32.5 (SD 6.1) to 20.5 (SD 10.4); 3 (50%) full responders, 1 partial responder, 2 non-responders; no post-operative complications.

DOI:10.1192/j.eurpsy.2026.11618.other_findings: One non-responder's inpatient days fell from 32% to 1% of time.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11395.topic: Equality and inclusion in adult autism assessment
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11395.setting: Skylight Psychiatry adult neurodiversity assessment service (NHS-commissioned and self-funded)
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11395.standard: NHS inclusion health principles, NICE guidelines and inclusive communication principles

cycle1.result: Strong representation of women, gender-diverse and LGBTQIA+ patients; lower than expected representation of some ethnic minority and religious groups; some inconsistent inclusive language in documentation (no figures given).

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11395.other_findings: Suggested actions include accessibility review of sites, easy-read and translated materials, and inclusion training.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keae163.043.setting: Airedale General Hospital rheumatology; patients on six-monthly denosumab

cycle1.result: 34/166 (21%) did not receive denosumab on time; 21/166 (12.6%) delayed and 13/166 (7.8%) missed; 8/166 (4.8%) sustained a fracture, 6 of whom had a delayed or missed dose during Covid-19.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keae163.043.other_findings: Reasons for delay were patient choice (44.1%), clinician safety decisions (35.3%) and clinical reasons (20.6%).

cycle1.result: Correct initial dose 28/28 (100%); level taken at correct time 13/15 (87%); 19/31 levels (62%) within 10–20 mg/L; all 6 levels >20 mg/L had next dose held, but follow-up adjustment often suboptimal; 3 of 4 low levels not acted on.

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2017-314584.13.intervention: Guideline amended (single safe range 10–20 mg/L, doses adjusted on levels not age) and teaching sessions with worked examples planned for prescribers and nurses.
DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2017-314584.13.other_findings: 19 patients had 28 courses and 31 levels. Levels appeared to be interpreted in isolation, causing avoidable repeat high levels.

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2023-nppg.23.topic: Ethanol line lock prescribing and documentation
DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2023-nppg.23.setting: Paediatric inpatients prescribed ethanol line locks
DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2023-nppg.23.standard: Trust paediatric ethanol line lock guideline (volume, concentration, indication, review, duration and consent documentation)

cycle1.result: 98% prescribed accurately per guideline; only 28% had documented indication, review and duration; 0 had consent documented.

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2023-nppg.23.intervention: Change to the electronic prescribing order suggested to aid documentation.
DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2023-nppg.23.other_findings: 36/46 (78%) line infections were eradicated and 40 (87%) did not need catheter removal; one adverse effect followed a prescribing error.

DOI:10.1192/j.eurpsy.2026.11710.setting: Stroke rehabilitation ward, Caerphilly, Aneurin Bevan University Health Board
DOI:10.1192/j.eurpsy.2026.11710.standard: NICE CG162 and Stroke Quality Standard QS2: 100% mood screening within 6 weeks, follow-up at discharge or 6–12 months, and all with depression offered treatment or referral

cycle1.result: not reported

DOI:10.1192/j.eurpsy.2026.11710.other_findings: Data collection was ongoing at the time of the abstract.

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2019-nppc.13.setting: Paediatric wards (patients ≥1 month) on intermittent IV vancomycin
DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2019-nppc.13.standard: Trust intermittent IV vancomycin guideline (2016) with loading dose and increased dose and frequency versus BNFC

cycle1.result: Pre-implementation audit: 7% of levels in therapeutic range at 48 hours; lack of support for appropriate dosing and monitoring.

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2019-nppc.13.intervention: New trust guideline for intermittent IV vancomycin (loading dose, higher dose and frequency) with pharmacist intervention.

cycle2.result: Loading dose used appropriately in 83%; levels at correct times in 90%; 40% in range at 48 hours; 100% reviewed at 48 hours; out-of-range levels reviewed per guideline in 40%, rising to 80% with pharmacist intervention.

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2019-nppc.13.other_findings: 30% still needed dose adjustment at 48 hours. Authors plan for pharmacist prescribers to adjust treatment directly.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11840.topic: Risk assessment on psychiatric admission and discharge
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11840.setting: Psychiatry inpatient unit, Gulab Devi Teaching Hospital, Lahore
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11840.standard: Risk assessment within 24 hours of admission covering all risk domains, risk management plan, and review and update before discharge

cycle1.result: Admission risk assessment within 24 hours 64%; documentation in notes 84%; risk from others 68%; risk management plan 72%; review before discharge 40%; update before discharge 40%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11840.intervention: Staff education, risk-assessment checklists displayed on the ward, and ward-round reminders.

cycle2.result: Admission risk assessment within 24 hours 92%; documentation 96%; risk from others 88%; risk management plan 88%; review before discharge 84%; update before discharge 80%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11840.other_findings: Audit ran over two months. Standardised admission and discharge proformas are recommended.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11847.topic: Factors associated with prolonged psychiatric length of stay
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11847.setting: Female acute psychiatric inpatient ward, East London NHS Foundation Trust
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11847.standard: NHS England ambition of about 32 days average acute adult mental health stay

cycle1.result: Mean LoS 29.76 days (SD 29.71), median 17 days (IQR 9–31); 40 (24.8%) stayed ≥32 days.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11847.other_findings: Prolonged stay was associated with Mental Health Act detention (aOR 6.07), schizophrenia-spectrum disorders (aOR 5.55) and mood disorders (aOR 4.77).

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11515.setting: South West London & St George's Mental Health NHS Trust; initial seclusion reviews by resident doctors
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11515.standard: Mental Health Units (Use of Force) Act 2018; target 80% compliance with all domains

cycle1.result: 75% of reviews met all required criteria.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11515.intervention: Four PDSA cycles: seclusion proforma made accessible at handover, proforma circulated by email, teaching in the academic programme, and small-group core trainee teaching.

cycle2.result: 83% of reviews met all required criteria; minimal change in overall compliance on SPC chart.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11515.other_findings: Small numbers and variation between on-call doctors caused wide fluctuations. Risk assessment and physical health documentation improved; authors suggest mandatory completion of all domains.

DOI:10.1192/j.eurpsy.2026.11149.setting: Two CAMHS learning disability services (Hereford and Worcester)

cycle1.result: Hereford (n=20) v Worcester (n=12): rationale documented 90% v 100%; reduce/stop plan 10% v 17%; MDT at initiation 30% v 67%; ongoing MDT review 0% v 0%; review ≤6 months 100% v 100%; monitoring complete 11/14 (79%) v 5/6 (83%); capacity/best interests 60% v 100%.

DOI:10.1192/j.eurpsy.2026.11149.other_findings: Planned actions include a mandatory medication review field in the MDT proforma, scheduled MDT follow-ups and standardised monitoring systems.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11563.topic: Medication prescribing in children with autism
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11563.setting: CAMHS across Black Country Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust localities
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11563.standard: NICE guidelines on psychotropic and sleep medication in children with autism

cycle1.result: Alternative interventions before medication 44%; consent documented 62%; follow-up within 3–4 weeks 70%; side effects recorded 61%; indication documented 83%.

cycle2.result: Alternative interventions 60%; consent 93%; follow-up within 3–4 weeks 75%; side effects 70%; indication 93%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11563.other_findings: Medications continued to be started at minimum effective dose. Recommendations include trust-wide clinic letter templates and consistent follow-up intervals.

PMID:29589502.topic: Supracondylar fracture nerve and vessel documentation
PMID:29589502.setting: Emergency departments of eight UK hospitals; re-audit in one hospital
PMID:29589502.standard: BOAST 11 standard 1: documented radial pulse, digital capillary refill time and individual radial, median (including AIN) and ulnar nerve function on presentation

cycle1.result: Nerve motor and sensory function documented in 201 (46%) to 232 (54%); radial pulse 318 (73%); capillary refill time 247 (57%).

PMID:29589502.intervention: Quality improvement proforma for emergency department assessment, piloted in one hospital.

cycle2.result: Nerve function documented in 72 (71%) to 80 (78%); radial pulse 84 (82%); capillary refill time 82 (80%).

PMID:29589502.other_findings: Only 44 (43%) of re-audit cases used the proforma; when used, adherence was 40 (91%) to 43 (98%) across all items.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2022.433.setting: All-male acute psychiatric ward, Livewell Southwest
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2022.433.standard: Lester UK Adaptation: Positive Cardiometabolic Health Resource (screening and action on red-zone risk factors)

cycle1.result: 50/63 had a Rethink template; of 41 smokers, 15 not offered cessation support; 28 of 31 with BMI >25 had no documented support; 8 of 12 hypertensive patients had no documented action; 27 of 32 with dyslipidaemia had no further intervention; 15 had no glucose test and 25 had no bloods.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2022.433.intervention: Changes to admission physical health assessments, well-man clinics and improved inpatient–community communication at discharge.
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2022.433.other_findings: 9 patients had no smoking status documented. Re-audit was pending.

DOI:10.1093/ageing/afaf368.069.topic: Anticholinergic burden reduction in older inpatients
DOI:10.1093/ageing/afaf368.069.setting: Acute Integrated Frailty Unit, Royal Liverpool University Hospital

cycle1.result: 28% (28/100) had ACB ≥3 on admission; 27% (27/100) still ≥3 at discharge; 33% of these readmitted at 3 months.

DOI:10.1093/ageing/afaf368.069.intervention: Automated Excel ACB calculator; frailty specialist nurses calculated pre-admission ACB scores on in-reach ward rounds and recorded them in electronic notes.

cycle2.result: 33.7% (27/80) had ACB ≥3 on admission; 30% (24/80) still ≥3 at discharge.

DOI:10.1093/ageing/afaf368.069.other_findings: A third cycle after a poster and teaching presentation is planned, with 3-month readmission rates.

DOI:10.1192/j.eurpsy.2025.2161.setting: Adult and older adult acute psychiatric inpatient wards, Cheshire and Wirral Partnership NHS Foundation Trust
DOI:10.1192/j.eurpsy.2025.2161.standard: Trust SOP 13 (Management of ligatures): every inpatient who ligatures should have a medical review

cycle1.result: Approximately 50% had a medical review after the ligature incident; 5/112 (about 4%), or 5/55 (9%) of those reviewed, had new management as a result.

DOI:10.1192/j.eurpsy.2025.2161.other_findings: No serious harm outcomes; medical input was minor (e.g. steristrips, CT after seizure). The authors question whether mandatory medical review is needed.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.136.topic: Functional status follow-up after rheumatoid arthritis rehabilitation
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.136.setting: Inpatient RA rehabilitation programme, Tallaght University Hospital and Peamount Hospital, Dublin
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.136.standard: EULAR treat-to-target: disease activity and functional status monitored every six months

cycle1.result: 33/36 (92%) completed six-month functional follow-up; median EQ-5D 46 at admission, 65 at discharge, 62.5 at six months; median self-efficacy 3.4, 7.0 and 5.5.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.136.other_findings: 45% had lower EQ-5D and 58% lower self-efficacy at six months than at discharge; home-exercise adherence was 79% and community support engagement 57%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10542.topic: Valproate prescribing in women of childbearing potential
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10542.setting: Hamad Medical Corporation psychiatric inpatient units
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10542.standard: MHRA and NICE guidance on valproate in women of childbearing age

cycle1.result: Teratogenicity discussion documented in 1 (3%); benefits 7 (21%); side effects 3 (9%); pregnancy test 21 (65.6%); contraception education 0.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10542.intervention: Results disseminated in the department and educational sessions for doctors and pharmacists.

cycle2.result: Teratogenicity discussion 10 (47.6%); benefits 5 (23.8%); side effects 14 (66.7%); pregnancy test 19 (90%); contraception education 8 (38.1%).

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10542.other_findings: Female bed capacity expanded during the re-audit. The audit prompted national guideline development and a QI project.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2022.492.topic: Obesity assessment in patients on antipsychotics
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2022.492.setting: Forensic community mental health team, supported accommodation, Cumbria, Northumberland, Tyne and Wear NHS Foundation Trust
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2022.492.standard: NICE obesity guideline (2014): BMI categorisation, waist circumference, lifestyle programme and interventions for risk factors

cycle1.result: 10/12 (83%) overweight or obese; only 4 had waist circumference measured; all overweight or obese patients received lifestyle advice; QRISK calculated for most eligible patients except two.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2022.492.other_findings: One patient was pre-diabetic and one diabetic.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keaa111.008.setting: East Kent Hospitals University NHS Foundation Trust (pathology requests from outpatients, inpatients and GPs)
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keaa111.008.standard: BSR Choosing Wisely recommendations on ANA testing

cycle1.result: Only 17% of requests met the standards; 41% inappropriate; 42% had insufficient details.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keaa111.008.intervention: Local ANA testing guidelines devised from Choosing Wisely standards.
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keaa111.008.other_findings: 180 (11.86%) tests were positive. Following the guidance could save about £12,000 a year; re-audit planned in 6 months.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10635.setting: Psychiatric rehabilitation and acute wards, Cygnet Churchill Hospital, London
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10635.standard: Carers Trust Triangle of Care partnership accreditation criteria

cycle1.result: Compliance 87% on rehabilitation wards and 68% on acute wards.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10635.intervention: Formalised stakeholder communication, more carer lead staff and carer awareness training, carer communication forms and logs, monthly carer events, and an infographic Carer Involvement Protocol.
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10635.other_findings: Cycle 2 (September 2024) also showed 100% adherence; carer event attendance rose by 28% and Triangle of Care accreditation was achieved in May 2024.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11659.topic: BMI monitoring in early intervention in psychosis
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11659.setting: Northamptonshire Early Intervention Psychosis Service (NSTEP North and South)
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11659.standard: National Clinical Audit of Psychosis EIP standards: routine BMI monitoring with intervention at BMI ≥25 (≥23 for South Asian and Chinese patients)

cycle1.result: 182/187 (97%) had BMI recorded; 64% overweight or obese (34% 25–29.9, 29% ≥30); 68% (13/19) of South Asian/Asian patients had BMI ≥23.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11659.other_findings: 68% (23/34) of Black Caribbean/African patients were overweight or obese; about half were on no antipsychotic or aripiprazole. Planned resource packs and links to exercise and diabetes prevention programmes.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.276.topic: Paget's disease of bone investigation and treatment
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.276.setting: All departments, University Hospital Southampton (including rheumatology and medicine for the elderly)
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.276.standard: Paget's Association, ECTS and IOF clinical guideline (February 2019)

cycle1.result: Targeted X-ray or CT in 127/143 (88.8%); bone scan in 38.4% (68.3% rheumatology v 22.6% other departments); ALP available in all rheumatology and 88.7% of other patients; bisphosphonates in 36.1% (73.3% rheumatology v 9.4% other).

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.276.other_findings: Bisphosphonates were mostly given for symptoms (65.4%) rather than ALP reduction. Targeted education for non-rheumatology specialties and re-audit are recommended.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10395.topic: Self-harm assessment in children and young people in the emergency department
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10395.setting: Emergency departments of nine teaching hospitals in Scotland, England and Wales

cycle1.result: Consent for family involvement documented in 73.5%; social media interactions documented in 21.5%; delayed psychosocial assessment in 17.8%; only 26.1% of 16–17-year-olds needing admission went to age-appropriate wards.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10395.other_findings: Student-led multicentre audit; further training for clinical teams recommended.
